articleHeader.title: Python Lambda Functions — The lambda Keyword Explained Properly
articleHeader.subtitle: Everything you actually need to know about Python's lambda — anonymous single-expression functions, how they differ from def, using them with map, filter, sorted, and reduce, and exactly where they stop being the right tool.

sections.title: What is a Lambda Function in Python?

blocks.text: A lambda function is a small, unnamed function you can write inline, in a single expression, without going through the full def name(): ceremony. lambda x: x * 2 is a complete, callable function — it takes one argument, doubles it, and hands the result back. No def, no function name, no return keyword even, because the expression's value is returned automatically.

The name comes from lambda calculus, a mathematical formalism from the 1930s that Python borrows the concept from (though not the notation — mathematicians write λx.x², Python writes lambda x: x**2). You don't need to know anything about lambda calculus to use this. It's genuinely just Python's syntax for a throwaway function you don't feel like naming.

Here's the thing most tutorials get slightly wrong about lambda: it isn't a different kind of function, and it isn't a shortcut for writing less code in general. It's specifically useful for exactly one situation — a small piece of function logic that another function needs as an argument, right where you're calling that other function, and that you'll never need to call by name anywhere else. sorted(students, key=lambda s: s['marks']) is the textbook case: you need a tiny 'get the sort key' function, you need it exactly once, right here, and giving it a name like get_marks just for this one call site would be more typing for zero benefit.

I've seen the opposite mistake plenty of times too — someone squeezing a genuinely complicated piece of logic into a lambda because they'd learned lambda existed and wanted to use it, producing something like lambda x: x['price'] * 0.9 if x['category'] == 'electronics' and x['stock'] > 0 else x['price'] crammed onto one unreadable line. That's not clever Python. That's a regular function that got squeezed into the wrong shape. This guide covers lambda's actual syntax, where it genuinely shines, how it interacts with closures, and — just as importantly — where a proper def function is the honest, correct choice instead.

sections.title: History — Where lambda Came From and Why It Almost Got Removed

blocks.text: Lambda's story in Python is genuinely interesting, because it's one of the few features Guido van Rossum has publicly said he regrets including in its current limited form — and there was a real, serious proposal to remove it entirely.

items.text: — lambda arrived alongside map(), filter(), and reduce() as part of Python's first real push toward functional-programming-style tools, borrowed conceptually from Lisp and other functional languages of the era.

— Unlike Lisp's lambda, which can contain multiple statements, Python's lambda was deliberately restricted to a single expression from the start, keeping it firmly in 'small inline helper' territory rather than a full alternative to def.

— In his early planning notes for Python 3.0, van Rossum seriously proposed removing lambda, map(), filter(), and reduce() entirely, arguing that list comprehensions and generator expressions covered the same ground more readably, and that functional-style one-liners didn't fit Python's design philosophy well.

— The proposal drew enough disagreement from the community that lambda, map(), and filter() were kept in Python 3.0, though reduce() was moved out of the builtins entirely and relocated to the functools module, requiring an explicit import — a genuine demotion in status.

— Shipped with lambda intact and unchanged, map() and filter() intact but now returning lazy iterators instead of lists (a separate change unrelated to lambda itself), and reduce() moved to functools.reduce().

— lambda remains exactly as restrictive and exactly as useful as it was in 1994 — a single-expression anonymous function, most commonly reached for as the key argument to sorted(), min(), max(), or inside pandas .apply() calls, and considered questionable style almost everywhere else.

blocks.text: lambda looks simple on the surface, but it has a precise, narrow set of behaviours. Here are the 10 things worth knowing exactly:

items.title: Single Expression Only
items.text: A lambda body must be exactly one expression — no statements, no if/else blocks with multiple lines, no loops, no assignments. lambda x: y = x + 1 is a SyntaxError, because assignment is a statement, not an expression.

items.title: Implicit Return
items.text: There's no return keyword in a lambda. Whatever the single expression evaluates to is automatically the return value — lambda x: x * 2 returns x * 2 without ever writing return.

items.title: Anonymous by Default
items.text: A lambda has no name of its own. Printing one directly shows something like <function <lambda> at 0x7f...>, which is why lambdas are almost always used immediately, in place, rather than stored and referenced by name later.

items.title: Can Be Assigned a Name
items.text: square = lambda x: x**2 assigns the lambda to a variable, which technically works and lets you call square(5). PEP 8 explicitly discourages this specific pattern — if you're naming it, use def instead.

items.title: Accepts Any Argument Style
items.text: lambda can take positional arguments, default arguments, *args, and **kwargs, exactly like a regular function — lambda a, b=10, *args: a + b + sum(args) is entirely valid syntax.

items.title: First-Class Function Object
items.text: A lambda is a genuine function object under the hood, with the same type(lambda: None) == <class 'function'> as a def-created function. It can be passed around, stored in data structures, and called like any other function.

items.title: Supports Closures
items.text: A lambda can reference variables from its enclosing scope, exactly like a nested def function — this is what makes lambda-based factory functions work, though it's also the source of a genuinely tricky late-binding gotcha.

items.title: Commonly Used as a Callback Argument
items.text: The overwhelming majority of real lambda usage is as an inline argument to another function — sorted(key=lambda ...), filter(lambda ...), pandas .apply(lambda ...) — not as standalone, independently useful code.

items.title: No Performance Difference from def
items.text: A lambda compiles to essentially the same bytecode as an equivalent def function. There's no speed advantage to choosing lambda — the only difference is syntax and where it's conventionally used.

items.title: Cannot Contain a Docstring
items.text: Since the body must be a single expression, there's no room for a triple-quoted docstring inside a lambda the way a def function can have one, which is one more reason lambdas are meant to stay small and self-explanatory rather than needing documentation.

sections.title: How a Lambda Gets Created and Called — Flowchart

blocks.text: A lambda expression goes through the same fundamental creation-and-call pipeline as any Python function — it's just compressed into one line with no name attached. Here's exactly what happens from the moment Python parses lambda x: x * 2 to the value it hands back when called.

Key insight: step 2 and step 4 happen at genuinely different times. The lambda is created once, the moment Python parses that line. It's called — potentially many times — later, whenever the outer function (like sorted() or map()) actually needs a value from it. This timing gap is exactly where the late-binding closure gotcha, covered further below, comes from.

sections.title: How lambda Actually Works — Syntax, Closures, and Common Uses

blocks.text: Three things separate someone who's memorised the lambda x: expr template from someone who genuinely understands it: the exact grammar rules for what can and can't go inside, how lambda behaves inside closures (including a real, well-documented gotcha), and the specific handful of situations where reaching for lambda is actually the right call versus where a named function would simply be clearer.
📝 The Exact Grammar — Why lambda x: if x > 0: return 1 Fails

Python's grammar draws a hard line between statements (things like if, for, return, assignment) and expressions (things that evaluate to a value, like x + 1 or a function call). A lambda body must be exactly one expression — nothing else is grammatically legal there. This is why lambda x: if x > 0: return 1 else: return -1 is a flat SyntaxError: invalid syntax — if...else... as a statement isn't allowed here at all. The correct way to get conditional logic into a lambda is Python's conditional expression (the ternary form): lambda x: 1 if x > 0 else -1. This is a single expression, not a statement, so it's completely legal — just visually similar enough to a regular if/else that beginners often write the wrong one first.
🧩 Closures and the Late-Binding Trap

A lambda created inside a loop can reference the loop variable — but here's the trap: it looks up that variable's value at call time, not at the moment the lambda was created. Write funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)] and call each function in funcs afterward, and every single one returns 2 — the loop's final value — not 0, 1, 2 as most people expect. This is because all three lambdas share the same enclosing variable i, and by the time any of them actually get called, the loop has already finished and i is sitting at its last value. The standard fix is forcing the current value to be captured immediately via a default argument: lambda i=i: i — using i as a default parameter value evaluates it right then, at creation time, not later at call time. This exact gotcha is not unique to lambda (regular nested def functions have the identical issue), but it shows up constantly in lambda code specifically because lambdas are so often created in loops or comprehensions.
🎯 The Genuinely Correct Uses of lambda

Lambda earns its place in exactly a handful of recurring patterns: providing a key function to sorted(), min(), or max(); a short predicate passed to filter(); a short transformation passed to map(); a quick callback for GUI event bindings; and one-off transformation logic inside pandas' .apply(). In every one of these cases, the lambda is small, used exactly once, right where it's defined, and never needs a name because nothing else in the program will ever call it independently.

Simple rule to remember: if you can write the lambda's logic in one short expression, and you're using it exactly once as an argument to another function, lambda is the right tool. If you find yourself squinting at a lambda trying to parse nested ternaries, or if you're assigning it to a variable so you can reuse it, switch to def — nothing is lost, and everything gets easier to read.
Every capability lambda has, def has too, plus more. The real question is never 'which one is more powerful' — def always wins that — it's 'which one fits this specific spot better.'

blocks.text: Here's my honestly opinionated take: Python's single-expression restriction on lambda is annoying at first and correct in the long run. JavaScript arrow functions and Java lambdas can silently grow into multi-line blocks of real logic buried inline inside a function call, which I've personally had to debug in codebases where a 'quick callback' had turned into forty lines of business logic nobody had bothered to extract into a named function. Python's grammar physically prevents that slow slide — the moment your logic needs more than one expression, you're forced to write a proper def function with a name, which is exactly the forcing function most other languages don't have.
lambda is genuinely useful in its narrow lane and genuinely harmful outside it. Here's the honest breakdown.

pros.title: Concise for Genuinely Simple Logic
pros.text: sorted(data, key=lambda x: x['age']) reads cleanly in one line, avoiding the ceremony of defining and naming a separate one-off function elsewhere in the file.

pros.title: Keeps Related Logic Visually Together
pros.text: The sorting/filtering rule sits right next to the call that uses it, rather than being defined somewhere else the reader has to jump to and back from.

pros.title: No Naming Overhead for Throwaway Logic
pros.text: Not every tiny piece of logic deserves a name that will never be reused — lambda avoids polluting a module's namespace with one-off helper function names.

pros.title: Genuine First-Class Function Object
pros.text: A lambda can be passed, stored, and called exactly like any other function — no special-case handling required by whatever accepts it.

pros.title: Supports Closures Just Like def
pros.text: Factory-style patterns that generate customised small functions work identically whether you use lambda or a nested def, giving flexibility in how you write that pattern.

pros.title: Zero Performance Cost
pros.text: There's no runtime penalty for choosing lambda over an equivalent def — the choice is purely about readability and convention, never about speed.

cons.title: Cannot Express Multi-Statement Logic
cons.text: The single-expression restriction means any real complexity has to be forced into ternaries and chained expressions, which quickly becomes harder to read than a proper function.

cons.title: No Docstring Support
cons.text: There's no way to document what a lambda does beyond the code itself — fine for truly obvious one-liners, a real loss for anything even slightly non-obvious.

cons.title: Debugging Tracebacks Are Less Helpful
cons.text: A traceback pointing to an error inside <function <lambda> at 0x...> is less immediately informative than one pointing to a properly named function.

cons.title: Late-Binding Closure Gotcha
cons.text: Lambdas created inside loops capture the loop variable by reference, not by value at creation time — a well-known, genuinely confusing trap for anyone unfamiliar with it.

cons.title: Tempts Overuse and Poor Readability
cons.text: Because lambda is available, some developers cram logic that clearly deserves a named function into an unreadable one-liner, purely because they can.

cons.title: Discouraged by Style Guides When Assigned a Name
cons.text: PEP 8 explicitly recommends against square = lambda x: x**2 — if you're naming it and reusing it, def is considered the honest, correct choice instead.

sections.title: lambda in Practice — From Basic Syntax to the Closure Gotcha

blocks.text: Here's lambda used correctly across its most common real patterns, followed by the exact late-binding trap and its fix.

blocks.label: lambda_basics.py
lines: # Sorting by a specific field using lambda as the key
ranked = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s["marks"], reverse=True)
# Filtering with lambda as the predicate
grades = list(map(lambda s: "A" if s["marks"] >= 85 else "B", students))

blocks.text: Now the late-binding closure trap — the exact bug, and the exact fix:

blocks.label: closure_trap.py
lines: # The trap — all three lambdas share the SAME variable i
broken_funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
# The fix — default argument captures the value immediately
fixed_funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]

blocks.text: Practice This Code — Live Editor

blocks.initialCode:
numbers = [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3]
squared_evens = list(map(lambda x: x**2, filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, numbers)))
print(squared_evens)

blocks.text: Line-by-Line Explanation

items.html: key=lambda s: s["marks"] — Gives sorted() a tiny function describing what to sort by, without needing a separate named get_marks(s) function defined elsewhere just for this one call.
filter(lambda s: s["marks"] >= 85, students) — The lambda acts as a predicate, returning True or False for each item; filter() keeps only the items where it returns True.
lambda s: "A" if s["marks"] >= 85 else "B" — A ternary conditional expression inside the lambda. This is legal because the whole if...else here is one expression, not a statement.
[lambda: i for i in range(3)] — Creates three separate lambda objects, but all three reference the exact same enclosing variable i by name, not by its value at creation time.

lambda i=i: i — The default argument i=i is evaluated immediately, at the moment each lambda is created inside that specific loop iteration, permanently capturing that iteration's value instead of a shared reference.

sections.title: Where lambda Actually Shows Up in Real Code

blocks.text: lambda has a genuinely narrow but real footprint across professional Python code. Here's exactly where it earns its place:

items.text: — sorted(records, key=lambda r: r['created_at']) is probably the single most common real-world lambda pattern — describing a sort key inline, without a separate named function that would only ever be used once.
— df['discounted'] = df['price'].apply(lambda p: p * 0.9) is an extremely standard pattern in data analysis scripts, applying a short transformation across an entire column.
— filter(lambda x: x.is_active, users) or the equivalent list comprehension are both common ways to express 'keep only the items matching this quick condition.'
— Tkinter and similar GUI libraries often use lambda to bind a button click to a function call with specific arguments: button.config(command=lambda: greet(name)).

items.strong: 🧮 Custom Comparators for min() and max()
items.text: — max(products, key=lambda p: p.rating) finds the highest-rated product without needing a standalone get_rating(p) function defined just for this one comparison.
— from functools import reduce; total = reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + x, numbers) folds a sequence down to a single accumulated value using a tiny inline combining function.
— In test code, lambda: True or lambda *args, **kwargs: expected_response are common quick stand-ins for real function behaviour that a test doesn't need to fully implement.

— A dictionary mapping string keys to small lambda functions — {'add': lambda a, b: a + b, 'sub': lambda a, b: a - b} — is a lightweight way to build a simple dispatch table without defining several small named functions elsewhere.

sections.title: Why lambda Deserves Careful Understanding, Not Blanket Avoidance

blocks.text: Some tutorials tell beginners to avoid lambda entirely, which overcorrects. Here's why understanding it properly — including its limits — actually matters:

items.strong: 📚 It's Everywhere in Real Library Code
items.text: — Sorting, filtering, and pandas transformations use lambda constantly in production codebases and open-source libraries. Not recognising the syntax makes reading real Python code genuinely harder.

items.strong: 💼 Interviewers Test Both Correct Use and Misuse
items.text: — Being asked to write a sort key using lambda, or being asked to spot why a lambda-in-a-loop produced wrong results, are both realistic interview scenarios covering this exact topic.
— Understanding exactly why lambda can't contain an if statement (but can contain a ternary expression) sharpens a genuinely useful mental model of Python's grammar that pays off elsewhere too.

items.strong: 🐛 The Closure Gotcha Is a Real, Recurring Bug Source
items.text: — Lambdas-in-loops producing identical, wrong results is a documented, common bug pattern — knowing the fix (default argument capture) is a practical debugging skill, not academic trivia.

items.strong: ✍️ Knowing When NOT to Use It Is a Real Code-Quality Skill
items.text: — Recognising when a lambda has grown too complex and should become a named def function is exactly the kind of judgment that separates readable codebases from cryptic ones.

items.strong: 🇮🇳 It's a Frequently Tested Topic in Indian Python Interviews
items.text: — Alongside list comprehensions and *args/**kwargs, lambda usage with sorted/filter/map is a standard, recurring theme in Indian campus placement and early-career Python interview rounds.

sections.title: lambda Paired With Python's Functional Tools

blocks.text: lambda rarely stands alone — its real value comes from pairing with a small set of higher-order functions. Here's how each pairing actually behaves:

items.text: — The key= parameter accepts any function that takes one item and returns a comparable value. lambda is the standard way to define that comparison logic inline, without a separate named function.

— filter() keeps items where the given function returns a truthy value. In modern Python, a list comprehension with an if clause ([x for x in items if x > 0]) is often considered more readable than filter(lambda x: x > 0, items) for simple cases — both work, but comprehensions have become the more idiomatic default.

— map() applies the given function to every item in an iterable. Similarly, a list comprehension ([x * 2 for x in items]) frequently reads more clearly than map(lambda x: x * 2, items) for simple transformations, though map() remains common, especially with existing named functions rather than lambdas.

— reduce() has no comprehension equivalent, so lambda genuinely earns its place here — folding a sequence down to a single value via repeated pairwise combination is exactly the kind of small, one-off logic lambda is meant for.

— Applying a lambda across a DataFrame column or row is extremely common in data analysis code, precisely because the transformation is usually short, specific to that one line, and not something you'd want cluttering the module's namespace as a named function.

blocks.text: These come up regularly in Python interviews, especially around sorting, functional-style code, and closures.

items.q: Q1. What is a lambda function in Python, and how is it different from a regular function?
items.a: A lambda function is an anonymous, single-expression function created with the lambda keyword instead of def. Unlike a regular def function, a lambda has no name of its own, cannot contain multiple statements or a docstring, and implicitly returns the value of its one expression without needing a return keyword.

items.q: Q2. Why can't a lambda contain an if/else statement, and what should you use instead for conditional logic?
items.a: A lambda body must be a single expression, and if/else as a statement is not an expression in Python's grammar — attempting it raises SyntaxError. The correct alternative is a conditional expression (ternary), written as value_if_true if condition else value_if_false, which IS a single expression and is fully valid inside a lambda.

items.q: Q3. What does sorted(data, key=lambda x: x['price']) actually do?
items.a: It sorts the data list, using the value returned by the lambda for each item as the comparison key — in this case, each item's 'price' field. Items with lower price values come first by default; passing reverse=True would sort from highest to lowest instead.

items.q: Q4. Explain the late-binding closure problem when creating lambdas inside a loop.
items.a: Lambdas created in a loop that reference the loop variable directly all share the SAME enclosing variable by reference, not by its value at creation time. By the time any of those lambdas are actually called, the loop has finished and the variable holds its final value — so every lambda returns that same final value, rather than the value it 'should' have captured during its own iteration. The fix is capturing the current value immediately using a default argument, like lambda i=i: i, which evaluates i right then rather than later.

items.q: Q5. Is there a performance difference between a lambda and an equivalent def function?
items.a: No meaningful difference. Both compile to essentially the same kind of function object and bytecode under the hood. The choice between lambda and def is purely about readability, convention, and whether the function needs a name — never about execution speed.

items.q: Q6. Why does PEP 8 discourage writing square = lambda x: x**2?
items.a: Because assigning a lambda to a variable name gains none of lambda's actual benefit — the whole point of lambda is to avoid naming a throwaway function used exactly once inline. If you're naming it and planning to reuse it, a regular def square(x): return x**2 is considered the clearer, more honest choice, and it also gains a docstring option and a cleaner traceback name.

items.q: Q7. Can a lambda accept default arguments, *args, or **kwargs?
items.a: Yes — a lambda supports exactly the same argument styles a def function does. lambda a, b=10, *args, **kwargs: a + b + sum(args) is entirely valid syntax, though piling on this much argument flexibility inside an anonymous, unnamed function is usually a sign it should be a proper named function instead.

items.q: Q8. What is the output of list(map(lambda x: x * 2, filter(lambda x: x > 2, [1, 2, 3, 4])))?
items.a: [6, 8]. filter() first keeps only values greater than 2 from the list, giving [3, 4], and then map() doubles each of those remaining values, producing [6, 8].

blocks.text: Work through these before checking the answers. Predicting exact output — including the closure trap — is the real test of understanding here.

items.q: 1. What is the output of: f = lambda x, y: x + y \n print(f(3, 4))
items.a: 7. The lambda takes two arguments and returns their sum via its single expression, with no explicit return keyword needed.

items.q: 2. What is the output of: print((lambda x: x ** 2)(5))?
items.a: 25. This is an immediately-invoked lambda — the lambda is defined and called in the same expression, using the extra parentheses to call it right away with 5 as the argument.

items.q: 3. Why does lambda x: print(x); return x raise a SyntaxError?
items.a: Two separate problems: first, a lambda body must be a single expression, and the semicolon here is trying to chain two separate statements together, which isn't valid inside a lambda at all. Second, return is itself a statement, not an expression, and is never valid inside a lambda body under any circumstances — a lambda's return value is always implicit.

items.q: 4. What does sorted(['banana', 'kiwi', 'apple'], key=lambda s: len(s)) return?
items.a: ['kiwi', 'apple', 'banana']. The lambda returns each string's length as the sort key, so the list is ordered from shortest to longest: 'kiwi' (4), 'apple' (5), 'banana' (6).

items.q: 5. Trace this: callbacks = [] \n for i in range(3): callbacks.append(lambda: i * 10) \n print([cb() for cb in callbacks])
items.a: [20, 20, 20]. All three lambdas share the same enclosing variable i by reference. By the time any of them are called, the loop has ended and i holds its final value, 2, so every lambda computes 2 * 10 = 20, regardless of which iteration created it.

items.q: 6. How would you fix the previous question so it prints [0, 10, 20] instead?
items.a: Capture the current value of i immediately using a default argument: callbacks.append(lambda i=i: i * 10). Since default argument values are evaluated at the moment the lambda is created (during that specific loop iteration), each lambda now permanently holds its own captured value of i rather than sharing one variable.

items.q: 7. What is the output of: from functools import reduce \n print(reduce(lambda acc, x: acc * x, [1, 2, 3, 4]))
items.a: 24. reduce() applies the lambda cumulatively: first combining 1 and 2 to get 2, then combining that 2 with 3 to get 6, then combining that 6 with 4 to get 24 — computing the product of all the numbers.

items.q: 8. What is the type of x = lambda: None, and what does calling x() return?
items.a: type(x) is <class 'function'> — a lambda is a genuine function object, identical in type to a def-created function. Calling x() executes the single expression None, and since that IS the value of the expression, it returns None.

sections.title: Conclusion — A Small Tool With a Genuinely Narrow, Correct Use

blocks.text: lambda is one of those features that's simultaneously overused by beginners excited to have found something that looks clever, and underused by developers who've been told to avoid it entirely and end up writing needlessly verbose named functions for genuinely trivial one-liners. The honest truth sits in between: lambda is exactly the right tool for a short, throwaway piece of logic passed inline as an argument, and exactly the wrong tool the moment that logic needs more than one expression, a docstring, or a name people will actually call directly elsewhere.

If you're a complete beginner, the priority is recognising lambda syntax when reading library code and being comfortable writing a simple key=lambda x: x.field pattern. If you're writing real, shared code, the priority shifts to judgment: knowing the exact moment a lambda has grown too complex, and switching to a properly named def function without hesitation the moment that happens.

blocks.text: The practical habit worth building: every time you write a lambda, silently ask whether you could read it back a week from now without slowing down. If the answer's no, it's not a lambda problem — it's a sign the logic deserves a real name and a proper def. That one-second check is the entire difference between lambda as a clean, idiomatic tool and lambda as the reason a code review takes twice as long as it should.

lambda is small on purpose. Respect that limit, and it stays one of the cleanest, most idiomatic tools in the language. Fight that limit, and it becomes exactly the kind of code nobody wants to touch six months later. 🐍

items.q: What is a lambda function used for in Python?
items.a: Lambda functions are used for short, throwaway logic needed exactly once as an argument to another function — most commonly as the key argument to sorted(), min(), or max(), or as the function passed to filter(), map(), or functools.reduce(). They're meant for small, single-expression logic, not general-purpose function writing.

items.q: Can a Python lambda function have multiple lines or statements?
items.a: No. A lambda's body must be exactly one expression — no if/else statements, no loops, no multiple lines, no assignment statements. Conditional logic is still possible using a ternary conditional expression (value_if_true if condition else value_if_false), since that form counts as a single expression rather than a statement.

items.q: What is the difference between lambda and a regular def function in Python?
items.a: lambda creates an anonymous, single-expression function with an implicit return and no name of its own. def creates a fully named function that can contain any number of statements, an explicit return, a docstring, and can be called by name from anywhere else in the program. Anything a lambda can do, def can also do — the reverse isn't true.

items.q: Why do all my lambdas inside a for loop return the same value in Python?
items.a: This is the well-known late-binding closure issue. Lambdas created inside a loop that reference the loop variable directly all share that same variable by reference, not by the value it held during their specific iteration. By the time any lambda is actually called, the loop has already finished, so every one of them reads the loop variable's final value. The fix is capturing the current value at creation time using a default argument, like lambda i=i: i.

items.q: Is using lambda faster than using a regular def function in Python?
items.a: No — there's no meaningful performance difference. Both compile to essentially equivalent function objects and bytecode under the hood. The choice between them is purely about code style, readability, and whether the function needs a reusable name, never about execution speed.

items.q: Why does PEP 8 recommend against assigning a lambda to a variable name?
items.a: Because doing so — like writing square = lambda x: x**2 — gains none of lambda's actual purpose, which is avoiding the need to name a function used exactly once inline. If a function is being named and potentially reused, PEP 8 recommends writing it as a proper def function instead, which also allows for a docstring and produces clearer tracebacks when something goes wrong inside it.
